andrew-li.text: Abstract

Nearly ¼ Canadian adults suffer from hypertension, but it’s often dismissed as “not serious” simply because there’s no symptoms until it triggers something worse. This article brings a clear and comprehensive analysis on what hypertension is and how to manage and live with it backed by peer-reviewed articles, meant for all ages. More importantly though, it powers readers with the knowledge that can change fear into action, which can help them in the present or the future and coincides with AiM’s mission of empowering health literacy.
Introduction

Imagine feeling completely fine at a routine check-up, then being told your blood pressure puts you at risk for serious disease. This happens to hundreds of millions of people each year, with the number of people diagnosed doubling between 1990 and 2019 NCD-RisC, 2021. Hypertension, also known as high blood pressure, rarely causes any symptoms at all, which perfectly explains its nickname “the silent killer”. Hypertension means that the force of blood pushing against your artery walls is consistently too high. Blood pressure is measured by the readings of two numbers: systolic (the pressure when your heart beats) over diastolic (the pressure when your heart rests between beats). For example, a reading of 120/80 means 120 systolic and 80 diastolic, which is often considered the borderline between normal and high blood pressure.

Nearly 1 in 4 Canadian adults live with this condition, and unfortunately, many don’t know about it Canada. When left untreated, it quietly damages the heart, kidneys, and blood vessels over the years, long before any symptoms may appear. By the time they do appear, it is often a sign of a much more serious disease Zhou et al. 2021. Understanding what hypertension is and how to catch it early is one of the easiest ways to protect your long-term health.
Causes/Risk Factors

Blood pressure rises and falls naturally throughout each day, going up when you exercise or feel stressed, and drops when you rest. Hypertension is diagnosed when these readings stay elevated consistently, not just in short jagged periods of time. There are two main types of hypertension. Primary hypertension develops gradually over many years and has no single cause since it’s linked to a mix of factors including age, genetics, diet, and lifestyle choices. Secondary hypertension is caused by an underlying condition, like kidney disease, for example, and tends to appear more suddenly. Primary is the most common out of the two, affecting around 90-95% of patients Mircea CINTEZA, 2014.

Luckily, there are measures that can be taken. Risk factors for hypertension fall into two categories: modifiable and non-modifiable. As the name suggests, modifiable factors are the ones that you can change. For example, diet choices like a high intake of salt, lack of consistent exercise, consumption of alcohol, smoking/vaping, and constant stress can all cause high blood pressure. By modifying these lifestyle choices, you can reduce your risk of hypertension by a lot. Non-modifiable factors are the risks that you cannot control. These include aging, genetics, and family history Cheraghi et al., 2025.
Signs and Symptoms

Most serious health conditions come with warning signs, so it's normal to expect the same from hypertension. However, hypertension breaks that rule entirely, being known as the “silent killer” because it usually causes no symptoms at all, even when blood pressure has been high for many years Cheraghi et al. 2025.

This is exactly what makes hypertension so dangerous. A person can feel completely healthy while on the inside, their blood vessels are slowly weakening day after day. Without any regular check-ups, high blood pressure can go unnoticed until it leads to a bigger problem, such as a heart attack or a stroke. By the time symptoms show up, they're often signs that damage has already occurred within the body.

Although people may report mild symptoms such as headaches or dizziness, virtually no patients feel standard day-to-day symptoms. In fact, studies show that 77% of diagnosed patients convince themselves they can feel it Granados-Gámez et al., 2015. Sometimes these symptoms are for another condition. This is exactly why routine checks are so important. Since the body doesn’t send warning signals, testing is the only reliable way to catch hypertension early on. A check doesn’t take a lot of time and can happen at your local pharmacy, a doctor’s office, or even at home with the appropriate equipment.

The takeaway from this is simple: you cannot feel your way to knowing your blood pressure. Regular checks and consistent monitoring is the tool that fills up the gap left by the lack of symptoms. Though it might seem tiring, it’s definitely a habit worth spending time building.
Diagnosis

Speaking of routine check ups, you may ask how hypertension is exactly diagnosed. Well, it isn’t complicated, but it still does need to be done the right way. Essentially, a medical professional will measure your blood pressure with a sphygmomanometer, which is a cuff-based device that squeezes the arm and tracks pressure as blood flows through it Cheraghi et al. 2025. The reading will show two numbers: systolic over diastolic pressure.

Now, a single high reading isn’t enough for a reliable diagnosis since blood pressure naturally rises and falls throughout the day depending on factors like stress, activity, and even how nervous someone may feel during the check up. That’s exactly why professionals take multiple readings on different days before confirming a diagnosis. The general threshold for hypertension is a reading of 130/80 mmHg or higher Cheraghi et al. 2025. mmHg is millimeters of mercury, and it’s the unit used to measure blood pressure. Readings below that threshold are considered normal or mildly elevated.

As mentioned earlier, there are factors that may impede the results. Therefore, to get an accurate reading, there are some simple conditions that need to be respected, such as sitting still and avoiding caffeine or exercise right before the test since they can all affect the acute blood pressure reading. Skipping these steps can throw off the results.

Because hypertension has no clear symptoms, diagnosis through a proper way is the only dependable way to catch its presence. Though a routine check up may seem simple, it still needs to be done correctly to avoid false information that might hurt instead of help.
Treatment and Management

The good news is that most causes of hypertension are modifiable, meaning they can be changed through everyday choices. That's why doctors call it the most prevalent yet modifiable cardiovascular risk factor Tokcan et al., 2024.

The most important line of treatment is lifestyle changes. For example, reducing sodium intake, eating more fruits and vegetables, getting consistent exercise, limiting alcohol and smoking (better yet, completely avoiding), and maintaining a healthy body weight all help lower blood pressure. These actions work since they reduce the strain/stress put on the blood vessels and the heart, which addresses the root of the problem rather than just scratching the surface.

However, when lifestyle changes aren’t enough on their own, medication comes into the frame. Common choices include diuretics, which help the body release excess sodium and water, as well as ACE inhibitors, which help relax the blood vessels and therefore ease the blood flow. It is important to keep in mind, however, that a doctor should be the one deciding which medication fits best for the person based on their overall health, how their body responds to treatment, and their medical history. The key takeaway is that hypertension isn’t something that happens to a person who is powerless to respond. With lifestyle adjustments and medical treatment, there are many real, proven, and effective tools that lend control back into the patient’s hands. It must also be said that managing this condition isn’t about completely eliminating it overnight; rather, it’s about steadily lowering the chance of harm through choices made every day.
Living with Hypertension
Managing hypertension long-term requires a few consistent habits. Incorporating them into your daily or weekly routine is key to controlling it over time.

Starting off, home monitoring is one of the most useful tools available. All that is required is to check blood pressure regularly at home using a simple at-home cuff. This way, both the doctor and the patient can track the results and identify changes early, which is extremely useful since hypertension itself doesn’t have any symptoms. Next is medication adherence. Make sure to consistently follow your doctor’s orders on how to take your medication. Even when you feel fine, never ever skip a dose, since even if it is occasionally, it can let blood pressure climb back to unsafe levels without any warning signs.

After that, there are dietary changes. This is all part of the lifestyle side of treatment discussed earlier. Finally, routine checkups with your doctor. Regular visits allow adjustment to medication, tracking of overall health, and reassurance that your treatment plan is on track. Please keep in mind that treatment plans are highly individualized, and you should always consult your personal physician before starting or modifying treatment.
Conclusion

So, to end off, make sure that you understand that hypertension isn’t dangerous because it’s an untreatable disease; rather, it’s dangerous because of its invisibility of symptoms and the fact that it's underestimated. Once you know how to look out for it, you’re once again in control of it.

bernardo-costa.text: Abstract

Mast Cell Activation Syndrome MCAS is an immune condition in which mast cells release excessive chemical mediators in response to ordinary, non-threatening stimuli, producing allergy-like symptoms across multiple organ systems. Because its presentation overlaps with many other conditions and no single test confirms it, MCAS is frequently missed or misdiagnosed, leaving patients to manage unpredictable flare-ups for years without a clear explanation. This article breaks down what is currently understood about the causes, symptoms, diagnostic criteria, and treatment options for MCAS, and offers guidance for patients navigating daily life with the condition, so that readers can better recognize the signs, engage in informed conversations with healthcare providers, and advocate for the care they need.
Introduction

Imagine your home's fire alarm going off at random times, triggered by useless things like a slight shift in temperature, a meal, or a stressful thought. For people living with Mast Cell Activation Syndrome MCAS, this can feel like their daily reality. MCAS is a condition affecting the immune system in which certain white blood cells, called "mast cells," become dangerously overreactive. Instead of defending the body from actual threats, they mistake everyday stimuli, or outside inputs, as a danger. This causes them to flood the body with a massive stream of chemicals and hormones directly into the bloodstream. This release leads to a host of chronic and acute allergy-like symptoms that can affect the entire body simultaneously. Medical research shows that the extent to which individuals are affected can vary wildly. Some people may be bedridden, while others experience only a slight inconvenience. Due to this variation and the similarities MCAS has to other diseases and allergies, it can be misdiagnosed by doctors. People may suffer for years without answers. Breaking down the complexities of MCAS into simple terms is a crucial step toward helping patients recognize their symptoms, advocate for their health, and secure a proper diagnosis.
Causes and Risk Factors

To understand what drives Mast Cell Activation Syndrome, it is vital to examine how our immune systems are wired to protect us. Mast cells serve as a frontline form of defence, positioned to detect and react to harmful invaders such as bacteria or toxins. In a healthy individual, these cells only release chemical signals when a legitimate threat is present. However, in an individual suffering from MCAS, these guards may react too easily, meaning that even a harmless stimulus can set them off Akin, 2017. Recent research suggests that specific cellular and genetic changes may contribute to some cases of MCAS rather than being the confirmed primary cause of the condition Özdemir et al., 2024. A key example involves mutations within a certain receptor (such as c-KIT responsible for controlling mast-cell growth and signalling. When this receptor mutates, it may cause mast cells to multiply abnormally and behave erratically. This can lead to the inappropriate release of chemicals and hormones even when the body is safe from harm Molderings et al., 2011; Özdemir et al., 2024. Furthermore, studies suggest that MCAS does not always exist in isolation.

Researchers have found some shared genetic patterns and similar symptoms between MCAS and other conditions. Most notably, MCAS has been associated with a condition called Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome POTS, which affects an individual's heart rate and blood pressure. This may point to broader problems in how the immune and nervous systems are regulated, which could make certain individuals more susceptible to developing the syndrome. However, information about whether MCAS can directly cause other conditions remains speculative Özdemir et al., 2024.
Signs & Symptoms

Because mast cells live inside almost every body tissue, especially those exposed to the outside, such as the skin, gut, and airways, a flare-up can strike anywhere at any time. Sometimes, an individual might experience symptoms across multiple body parts at once. This unpredictable nature is what makes the condition extremely disruptive to daily life. On the outside, a flare-up may look like a usual allergic reaction, causing sudden skin redness, hives, or swelling. Internally, it can manifest as severe stomach aches, nausea, diarrhoea, or abdominal distress Castells et al., 2024. However, the impact of MCAS goes beyond typical physical allergy symptoms. Many people suffer from significant neurological and psychological symptoms, most often a profound impairment of cognitive abilities, such as brain fog Castells et al., 2024. This means that, alongside the physical discomfort, people with MCAS may struggle with memory loss, concentration issues, and mental fatigue during a flare-up. These difficulties can often resemble ADHD-like symptoms Castells et al., 2024.
Diagnosis

Getting an official diagnosis of MCAS is difficult because its symptoms mimic other illnesses and there is no single unique symptom. To make matters worse, routine blood work and medical scans are ineffective for identifying the illness on their own. For a patient to find answers, a doctor must first suspect MCAS and then work through a long and strict checklist of criteria.

According to medical consensus, a formal diagnosis of MCAS requires meeting three specific criteria Valent et al., 2018 1. Episodic Symptoms: Severe, recurring symptoms affecting two or more organ systems at the same time.

2. Tryptase Spike: A blood test must show a rise in serum tryptase (a specific enzyme released by mast cells) taken during an active flare-up. This spike is measured against the patient's baseline level, specifically calculated as a 20% increase plus 2 ng/mL over baseline.
3. Clinical Response: The patient must show clear, obvious improvement when administered medications that target these chemical mediators.
Note: Symptoms vary widely between individuals; readers should not self-diagnose based on this list. If someone suspects they have this condition, they should consult a healthcare provider.
Treatment & Management

Although there is currently no cure for MCAS, there are several forms of treatment that can help control symptoms and reduce the severity of flare-ups. Since the condition affects each individual differently, there is no single medication that works for everyone. Instead, treatment is often based on the specific chemicals being released by the mast cells and the symptoms they are causing. The most common treatments for MCAS are antihistamines. H1 antihistamines are generally used to reduce symptoms involving the skin, such as itching, hives, and swelling. H2 antihistamines can be used to control symptoms affecting the digestive system, such as stomach pain, nausea, or acid reflux. Furthermore, medications known as mast cell stabilizers can be used to prevent mast cells from releasing large amounts of chemicals into the body in the first place Weiler et al., 2019. In more serious cases, stronger medications may be considered when the patient continues to experience severe or frequent reactions. If a flare-up develops into anaphylaxis—a severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction, epinephrine must be administered as quickly as possible. Although antihistamines may reduce certain symptoms, they cannot replace epinephrine during a serious emergency Weiler et al.,2019.
Emphasize: Treatment plans are highly individualized; readers should always consult their personal physician before starting or modifying treatment.
Living with MCAS

Living with MCAS can be extremely difficult because flare-ups are often unpredictable and may be caused by normal parts of everyday life. Certain foods, medications, exercise, changes in temperature, and even emotional stress may cause the mast cells to react. However, triggers vary wildly between patients, meaning something that causes a severe reaction in one person may cause no reaction in another. Due to this, identifying personal triggers is an important part of managing the condition. Many individuals record their symptoms, meals, activities, and medications in order to determine whether a pattern exists. This information can then be shared with a doctor, helping both the patient and the medical professional create a more effective and personalized treatment plan. Furthermore, individuals at risk of experiencing anaphylaxis may be required to carry epinephrine and have an emergency plan prepared. Avoiding confirmed triggers and taking medication as prescribed can reduce the number of flare-ups. However, because MCAS can change over time and affects every patient differently, consistent communication with a medical professional remains vital to safely living with the condition Weiler et al., 2019. Conclusion Mast Cell Activation Syndrome is a complex condition where mast cells become dangerously overreactive and release large amounts of chemicals even when the body is not facing an actual threat. Since these cells exist throughout almost every body tissue, the symptoms can affect multiple organs simultaneously and vary significantly between individuals.

The condition is especially difficult to diagnose because its symptoms closely resemble those of allergies and several other illnesses. In order to receive an official diagnosis, an individual must experience repeated symptoms across multiple organs, show measurable evidence of mast cell activation, and improve after receiving medications that target the chemicals being released. Although there is currently no cure for MCAS, treatments such as antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, and emergency epinephrine can help patients control their symptoms and prevent serious reactions. Research surrounding the condition is still developing, meaning its exact causes and connections with conditions such as POTS are not yet fully understood. Increasing awareness and breaking down the complexities of MCAS into understandable terms can help individuals recognize their symptoms, communicate with doctors, and advocate for the medical care they require.

elia-ma.text: Abstract

Ebola can begin with symptoms that look like a common illness, a fever, headache and tiredness, but it can quickly become a serious medical emergency. This article explains what Ebola virus disease is, how it spreads, its symptoms, how it is diagnosed, and how it can be treated and prevented by understanding the warning signs and why a fast response matters, readers can better understand how Ebola outbreaks are controlled and how medical advances have improved patient outcomes.
Introduction

Imagine waking up, with a high fever, a pounding headache and overwhelming exhaustion. At first, you think it’s just the flu, so you stay home and try to rest. As the hours pass, your symptoms worsen instead of improving, and you begin to realize that something is seriously wrong. For people infected with Ebola, this isn’t just a possibility: it becomes a frightening, life threatening medical emergency that requires immediate treatment, and getting medical help quickly can make the difference between life and death.

Ebola virus disease EVD is a rare but severe viral illness caused by viruses in the Ebolavirus family. Ebola spreads through direct contact with infected body fluids, such as blood, vomit, urine, or saliva, especially during close contact with someone who is infected. Additionally, it does not spread through the air like the common cold or flu. People with Ebola are generally not contagious until they begin showing symptoms Rojek et al.). Early warning symptoms include fever, headache, fatigue, muscle pain, and sore throat. Because these symptoms are similar to those of many common illnesses, Ebola can be difficult to recognize in its early stages. As the disease progresses, people may develop vomiting, diarrhea, a rash and in severe cases, internal or external bleeding.

Understanding Ebola is important because knowing the early warning signs can help people seek medical care sooner and reduce the spread of the virus. Quick action through early diagnoses, patient isolation, contact tracing, and proper medical treatment can help save multiple lives and prevent outbreaks from spreading and becoming bigger.

Prevention methods include practicing good hand hygiene (ex: washing hands), avoiding contact with infected body fluids, and using Personal Protective Equipment. By learning how Ebola spreads, how it is treated, and how outbreaks are controlled, readers can better understand the importance of public health and the advances in medical research that continue to improve the survival and outbreak response.
What is Ebola Virus?

Ebola virus is a type of virus that infects human cells and weakens the immune system, which is the body’s natural defense against infections. Once the virus enters the body, it starts infecting healthy cells and makes copies of itself very quickly. This weakens the immune system, which is the body’s natural defense against infections, and can eventually damage important organs if the infection becomes severe Bodmer et al.).

One thing that is important to understand is that Ebola does not spread through the air like a common cold or the flu. Instead, it spreads through direct contact with the body fluids of someone who has Ebola, especially during close contact. These fluids can include blood, vomit, urine, or saliva. Ebola can also spread through contaminated objects, such as needles or medical equipment that have not been cleaned properly Frankfurter et al.). Because of this, people caring for someone who is sick or working closely with infected patients can have a higher risk of exposure.

Some people are at a higher risk of getting Ebola than others. Healthcare workers, family members, and care givers often have the greatest risk because they may come into close contact with an infected person’s body fluids. During an outbreak, simple prevention methods can help and make a big difference. Wearing Personal Protective Equipment PPE, such as gloves, masks, gowns and face shields, washing your hands, cleaning contaminated surfaces, and isolating infected patients all help reduce the spread of the virus. Responding quickly by testing people early, tracing their close contacts and providing medical care can also help stop outbreaks before they become larger Frankfurter et al.).
Signs and Symptoms

The first symptoms of Ebola usually appear between 2 and 21 days after a person has been exposed to the virus. At first, the symptoms can seem like many other common illnesses, which is one reason why Ebola can be so difficult to recognize early on. Someone with Ebola may develop a fever, headache, extreme tiredness, muscle pain and a sore throat. Since these symptoms are so similar to illness like the flu, many people may not realize they have Ebola right away Rojek et al.).

As the infection gets worse, symptoms become much more serious. A person may begin to experience vomiting, diarrhea, and a rash. In severe cases, Ebola can also cause internal or external bleeding. However not everyone with Ebola experiences bleeding, especially during the early stages of the disease. This is why doctors look at a person’s symptoms along with their recent travel history or possible exposure to the virus before deciding on the next steps.

Recognizing the warning signs early is very important. The sooner someone receives medical care, the sooner doctors can begin treatment and take steps to reduce the spread of the virus. Early recognition can also improve a person’s chances of survival and help protect others from being infected Rojek et al.).
Diagnosis

Diagnosing Ebola is not always easy because many of the early symptoms are similar to other illnesses, such as the flu. Because of this, doctors cannot diagnose Ebola based only on symptoms. They can also consider whether the person has travelled to an area experiencing an outbreak or has been in contact with someone who has the virus.

To confirm an Ebola infection, doctors commonly use a laboratory test called RT-PCR Reverse Transcription Polymerase Chain Reaction). This test detects the genetic material of the virus in a blood sample and helps doctors confirm whether someone has Ebola. Once a diagnosis is confirmed, patients can be isolated and treated as quickly as possible Rojek et al.).

Another important part of controlling Ebola outbreaks is contact tracing, which means identifying and monitoring people who have been in close contact with an infected person. This allows health officials to find new cases earlier and reduce the spread of the virus. Early diagnosis, together with contact tracing and patient isolation plays an important role in controlling outbreaks Muzembo et al.).
Note: Symptoms vary widely between individuals; readers should not self-diagnose based on this list. If someone suspects they have this condition, they should consult a healthcare provider.
Treatment and Management

There is no simple cure for Ebola, so treatment focuses on supporting the body while it fights the infection. Supportive care may include giving fluids to prevent dehydration, providing oxygen when needed, replacing electrolytes, which are minerals that help the body function properly, and treating complications that develop.

Another treatment doctors may use is monoclonal antibody therapy. Monoclonal antibodies are lab-made proteins that help the immune system recognize and fight the Ebola virus more effectively. However, while treatments such as monoclonal antibody therapies and supportive care have improved survival, access to these treatments can depend on where an outbreak occurs and the availability of healthcare resources. These treatments have improved patient outcomes, especially when they are given early in the illness El Ayoubi et al.).

Vaccines have also made a big difference in reducing the impact of Ebola outbreaks although current vaccines only protect against certain strains of the virus, they have helped lower the numbers of infections in recent outbreaks. First along with supportive care, early diagnosis, and strong Public Health measures, vaccines continue to improve survival and can help control the spread of Ebola. Access to treatments and other medical resources can also vary depending on where an outbreak occurs and what healthcare resources are available in that area El Ayoubi et al.; Rojek et al.). Emphasize: Treatment plans are highly individualized; readers should always consult their personal physician before starting or modifying treatment.
Conclusion

Ebola is a serious disease, but understanding how it spreads and recognizing its symptoms can help people respond appropriately. Fast diagnosis, proper medical care, prevention measures, vaccines, and continued research all play an important role in controlling outbreaks. By learning the facts about Ebola, readers can better understand the disease without unnecessary fear and recognize why a fast and informed response matters El Ayoubi et al.; Rojek et al.).

gerald-szeto.text: Abstract

Antibiotic resistance could make once-treatable infections significantly more difficult to treat, threatening millions of lives and modern medicine procedures. This article explains the development and spread of bacterial resistance, why it threatens the healthcare system and how the misuse of antibiotics accelerates this challenge. By simplifying complex science into practical information, this article helps patients understand that bacteria, not people, become resistant to antibiotics. It also shows how responsible antibiotic use and infection prevention can help preserve these life-saving medicines for future generations.
Introduction

Antibiotics have transformed modern medicine, turning once-deadly infections into treatable conditions. However, widespread use and misuse have contributed to a growing global health crisis by giving bacteria more opportunities to evolve and survive antibiotic treatment.

Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria change, reducing or eliminating the effectiveness of antibiotics. A common misconception is that people become resistant to antibiotics. In reality, it's the bacteria that evolve to survive these medicines, making infections increasingly difficult to treat.

As antibiotic resistance spreads, even common infections can become deadly, and many medical procedures that rely on effective antibiotics become riskier. Without effective antibiotics, millions of lives could be lost, and the global economy could face trillions of dollars in losses.
How Does Antibiotic Resistance Develop?

How does this happen? Imagine spraying a garden full of weeds with weed killer. Most of the weeds die, and your garden looks great. But a few survive due to naturally occurring traits that allow them to withstand the spray. Before long, the weeds come back. You use the spray again, but this time, they survive and thrive. Bacteria behave similarly: when antibiotics are used, most bacteria are killed, but a small number may carry genetic traits that make them more resistant to the drug. These bacteria multiply and pass their resistance traits to future generations, making antibiotics less effective over time. This process is called natural selection, where organisms with helpful traits are more likely to survive and reproduce.

Through random genetic mutations and the exchange of resistance genes, some bacteria naturally develop ways to survive antibiotics. However, the overuse and misuse of antibiotics can accelerate this process by giving resistant bacteria more opportunities to survive and multiply. For example, antibiotics do not work against viral infections, like the common cold or flu, because they only target bacteria. Using them for these illnesses provides no benefit to the patient while still exposing bacteria to the drug, creating an opportunity for resistant bacteria to survive. Similarly, skipping doses or stopping treatment early may leave some bacteria alive, including those that are more resistant to the antibiotic. Taking leftover antibiotics can also be harmful because the medication may be the wrong type or dose for the infection, allowing bacteria to survive rather than being effectively eliminated.

Antibiotic resistance isn't limited to hospitals nor doctor’s offices. In many countries, an estimated 70-80% of medically important antibiotics are used in agriculture to treat and prevent disease in livestock. These bacteria and their resistance genes can spread to humans through food, direct contact with animals, or contaminated water and soil. This relationship works both ways: wastewater from hospitals, farms, and pharmaceutical manufacturing can also carry resistant bacteria into the environment, allowing resistance genes to move between humans, animals, and ecosystems.
Why Is Antibiotic Resistance a Growing Concern?

The transmission of resistant bacteria between ourselves and the environment makes antibiotic resistance more than an individual health problem. Once these resistant germs spread through communities, they become nearly impossible to control.

Infections that were once treated with simple antibiotics now require stronger antibiotics, longer hospital stays, or no effective treatment at all. As a result, antibiotic resistance is now considered one of the most serious threats to global health.

These consequences extend far beyond everyday infections. Many modern medical procedures depend on antibiotics to prevent or treat infections before, during, or after treatment. Surgeries, organ transplants, chemotherapy, and even the care of premature babies rely on antibiotics to keep hundreds of millions of people safe. This puts a heavy burden on healthcare systems as infections become harder to treat. This can lead to longer hospital stays, higher medical costs, and an increased risk of death. Bacteria are evolving faster than new antibiotics can be developed, creating a gap between the growing need for effective treatments and the development of new ones. Developing a new antibiotic can take 10 to 15 years from initial laboratory discovery to patient availability. This long development process makes it difficult to keep pace with the spread of antibiotic resistance.

Because of this challenge, researchers are exploring new ways to prevent and treat resistant infections. One promising approach is phage therapy, which uses viruses called bacteriophages to infect and destroy specific bacteria. However, phage therapy is still being studied and is not yet widely used in routine clinical practice. Researchers are also developing faster molecular diagnostic tests that can identify resistant bacteria within hours instead of days, helping doctors choose the most effective treatment sooner. While these approaches may expand our options in the future, preventing antibiotic resistance remains a critical part of addressing the problem. (Aslam, Bilal, et al.; Nadgir, Chinmayee A, and Dalia A Biswas.)
What Can You Do to Help?

While antibiotic resistance is a global issue, individual actions can make a meaningful difference. Antibiotics should only be taken when prescribed by a healthcare professional and should never be used for viral illnesses as they only work against bacteria. If antibiotics are prescribed, they should be taken exactly as directed, even if you start feeling better. Do not share prescriptions or save leftover antibiotics for future illnesses, as the wrong antibiotic or an incorrect dose may not effectively treat an infection and can contribute to resistance. If you are unsure whether you need antibiotics or have concerns about your treatment, talk with your healthcare provider. Asking questions and having an open conversation can help you understand why an antibiotic is or is not recommended and how to use it safely.

Preventing infections is another key way to reduce the need for antibiotics. Regular handwashing, staying up to date with recommended vaccinations, practicing safe food handling, and seeking medical advice when symptoms worsen can all help lower the spread of bacterial infections. Patients can also play an active role by asking questions like whether an infection is bacterial or viral and whether antibiotics are truly necessary. By using antibiotics responsibly and staying informed, everyone can help slow the spread of antibiotic resistance and preserve these life-saving medicines for future generations.
Note: If you have questions about whether you need antibiotics or how to use them, speak with a healthcare professional. Do not start, stop, or change antibiotic treatment without medical guidance.
Conclusion

Antibiotic resistance is one of the greatest challenges in modern medicine, but it's not impossible to overcome. By understanding how resistance develops, why it threatens healthcare around the globe, and how our everyday choices affect its spread, we can all play a role in protecting the antibiotics that have saved countless lives.

Every decision matters. Only use antibiotics when they're truly needed, follow your healthcare provider’s instructions, and continue practicing habits that prevent infections in the first place. Together, small actions taken by millions of people can help preserve these life-saving medicines for future generations.

isabella-wang.text: Abstract

When will the next seizure occur? How will it happen? Fear, anxiety, depression. Three factors that surround epilepsy patients every day. Not knowing when the next seizure will occur, how people around them will react, and the fear of losing their lives are challenges that people living with epilepsy face every day. Numbers are increasing as ⅓ of epilepsy cases go untreated for up to 3 years after diagnosis Push10 Webmaster) and 70% of patients could live seizure-free if properly treated and diagnosed World Health Organization). Through research-based explanations, this article explores the causes, symptoms, diagnosis, treatments, and lifestyle guidelines for living with epilepsy. So let’s give hope to these patients: the hope for a better future and the understanding that epilepsy doesn’t define who they are.
Introduction
“Dear Epilepsy, Just so you know, I won’t give up. I won’t give in. I have endless hope.
Endless faith. You may be in my life. But you don’t own my life Epilepsy Network).

According to NIH PubMed, epilepsy is the 4th most common brain disorder and affects around 65 million people worldwide. It is made up of recurring and unprovoked seizures caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain. There are 3 types that distinguish the severity of the seizure: generalized epilepsy, where both sides of the brain are affected; focal epilepsy, with only one affected area of the brain; and unknown, where the major source of activity is not identified.

For millions of people affected by epilepsy, these seizures happen unexpectedly and sometimes without any warning signs. Untreated epilepsy can result in various life-threatening factors, from social disability to death. Since seizures are unpredictable, friends and family that are surrounding the epilepsy patients are a significant contributor in helping manage their fears. According to NIH PubMed, epilepsy causes a 4-7 times higher mortality rate than others because of the major source of electrical activity. So let’s give these patients the chance to explore the world by creating a safe environment for all.
Causes

Firstly, what causes epilepsy and what are the risk factors that increase the chances of being diagnosed with this medical condition? According to Epilepsy Research Institute UK, 65% of people living with epilepsy are not aware of the causes of their diagnosis. The remaining 35% are generally caused by anything that disrupts the normal pattern of nerve cell activity in the brain: genetic influence, developmental conditions, and head trauma.

Genetic influence, whether it is inherited or a change to a gene’s DNA sequence, plays a major role in epilepsy diagnosis. For example, a type of epilepsy is the channelopathy-associated epilepsy. This is when the DNA sequence changes the ion channels, which are proteins that control the signals of the neurons in the brain NIH.
When modified, multiple seizures are triggered because the neurons become hyperexcited and fire too frequently.

Developmental conditions, like Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (also known as ADHD, are shown to increase children’s risk of certain types of epilepsy. This includes generalized epilepsy (where the whole brain is affected) and frontal lobe epilepsy (where there is only one affected part of the brain) Ahmed et al., 2022. A study from the International League Against Epilepsy shows that ADHD was present in 30-40% of epileptic children. This is because people diagnosed with this disorder may have functional abnormalities in multiple areas of the brain that disrupt the pattern of the nerve cell activity. Other relationships that are common between ADHD and epilepsy patients are inflammation, anxiety, and stress.

Post-traumatic epilepsy PTE is the type of epilepsy developed after a traumatic brain injury TBI, also known as head trauma. It can be an immediate seizure that happens within twenty-four hours of the injury, an early seizure that is less than a week, or a late seizure after a week of the injury Kan Ding et al., 2016. A seizure occurs because the brain is traumatized, inflamed, and disrupted. For these reasons, there are multiple factors that trigger epilepsy, from genetics to daily lifestyles.
Signs & Symptoms

So what are the warning signs of a seizure or epilepsy? How can the people surrounding you as well as yourself be prepared? Since each person’s brain functions differently, the body reacts in various ways. Therefore, the signs, symptoms, and the type of seizure all depend on the person Mayo Clinic, 2025.

General symptoms that might occur during an epileptic seizure include a short-term confusion, stiff muscles, and emotional distress like fear, anxiety, or déjà vu Mayo Clinic, 2025. Emotional distress mostly happens to patients with focal epilepsy, which, as mentioned above, affects one part of the brain: the temporal lobe. This lobe is responsible for short-term memory and processing emotions Mayo Clinic, 2025.
Thus, with the temporal lobe affected, it causes the patient’s body to react with these symptoms.

The signs that are visible to the people surrounding the patient are a brief moment when the person doesn’t move or respond, jerking movements of arms and legs, and a loss of consciousness Mayo Clinic, 2025. During an epileptic seizure, patients might lose consciousness as the areas of the brain responsible for thinking and awareness are malfunctioning Blumenfeld & Taylor, 2003. Some patients might experience jerking movements because of the muscles that contract repeatedly NIH. This is because there is an excessive firing of electrical signals in the brain that overwhelm its communication with the body’s muscles.
Note: Symptoms vary widely between individuals; readers should not self-diagnose based on this list. If someone suspects they have this condition, they should consult a healthcare provider.
Diagnosis

Epilepsy or seizure? With the rapid advancement of technology, the medical field has developed various testing methods to diagnose different patients and improve their quality of life: electroencephalography EEG, neuroimaging MRI scans), and single-photon emission computerized tomography SPECT.

Electroencephalography, also known as EEG, is a testing method that records the brain’s electrical activity. During an EEG test, electrodes (electrical conductors) are placed on the patient’s scalp, allowing health professionals to monitor the patient’s brain activity during sleep or speech. If the patient is diagnosed with epilepsy, the EEG amplitudes will increase compared to an unaffected human being because of the rapid and uncontrollable neuronal discharge Blinowska, 2006.

Neuroimaging, which includes MRI scans (magnetic resonance imaging) of the brain, is shown to be very efficient in identifying epilepsy. Other imaging methods like CT scans (computerized tomography) show a less detailed view of the patient. According to NIH, MRI scans were able to successfully diagnose 80% of focal epilepsy patients Roy & Pandit, 2011. Unfortunately, this type of brain scanning is unavailable for a large number of patients because of its elevated cost and the long scanning period.

Single-photon emission computerized tomography, also known as SPECT, is another type of medical imaging of the brain. This method is used if both CT and MRI scans weren’t able to identify the origin of the seizure. SPECT is performed through injecting a low dose of radioactive substance into the vein of the patient. The contrast creates a 3D map of the blood flow, which shows which part of the brain receives a higher amount of blood and most likely identifies the source of the seizures. By visualizing the internal functions, it can help doctors further investigate the patient’s diagnosis Mayo Clinic, « Epilepsy - Diagnosis and Treatment - Mayo Clinic », 2025.
Treatment and Management

But what can I do as an epilepsy patient or as a friend or family member of someone going through epilepsy? Living with this condition can be tough, but many factors from lifestyles to drugs to surgeries have been adapted to enrich the quality of their lives Perucca et al., 2018.
Antiepileptic drugs, also known as AEDs, are the main approach to epilepsy treatment.

According to PubMed NIH, antiepileptic drugs help ⅔ of newly diagnosed patients reduce seizures. Without disturbing any non-epileptic activity and normal function of the nervous system, these drugs modify the excitement of neurons. This reduces uncontrolled activity in the brain by using sodium and calcium channels, which are proteins that control the electrical activity in the body Rogawski & Löscher, 2004.

According to Wiley, if two appropriate trials of this drug have failed, epilepsy surgery is the alternative treatment Perucca et al., 2018. This may be because of the patient having drug-resistant epilepsy, where medication no longer works in treating the disorder. In terms of surgery, there are many types of procedures that can be performed based on the type of epilepsy and the degree of severity: resective surgery, which removes the part of the brain where the seizures originated; and Multiple Subpial Transection, known as MST, where brain tissue is cut to disrupt the spread of seizures Patient Education Library).

For patients where surgery has failed to treat epilepsy, lifestyle therapies have been developed to control these seizures. For instance, the ketogenic diet is an option recommended mostly for children. This diet includes a heavier intake of glucose and ketones. Glucose is a sugar used to be converted to energy, while ketones are chemicals the body produces to break down fat into energy. Thus, this meal plan is made to promote the production of energy through healthy fat and reduced carbohydrates Saxena & Nadkarni, 2011.
Note: Treatment plans are highly individualized; readers should always consult their personal physician before starting or modifying treatment.
Living With Epilepsy

What can you do to protect yourself and others around you in case of an epileptic seizure? Or in prevention of one? A healthy lifestyle, following the medication, and avoiding unprescribed medicine all shape the recommendations involved with improving the quality of life when living with epilepsy Murray, 2017.

First, taking the prescribed amount of medication made by your doctor is important to assure a constant routine. Next, a healthy lifestyle is important to reduce stress, such as increasing sleep, following a balanced diet, and decreasing harmful use of drugs or alcohol. Additionally, avoiding medications that can possibly increase the severity of the condition can pose greater benefits Murray, 2017. For example, certain antibiotics may interact harmfully with anti-seizure medications or even antidepressants (found in 30-50% of epilepsy patients according to NIH PubMed).

Among the causes of this condition, there are factors that you should be aware of to prevent epilepsy: traumatic brain injury TBI and stroke. Traumatic brain injury is caused by an outside force like a blow to the head during sports injuries or if an object enters the brain tissues National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke). It is the cause of epilepsy for around 5% of total cases and is most common in children because they tend to have thinner and softer skulls Thurman et al., 2020. So next time you do a sport (especially combat sports), don’t forget to protect yourself.

Stroke occurs when the brain has less access to oxygen and nutrients because of the interrupted blood flow. This factor is most common for older adults in 19-24% of cases because as they age, they tend to have stiffer blood vessels and an overall decline in the heart’s health. For all ages, high blood pressure and high cholesterol all increase the chances of epilepsy. Therefore, although half of epilepsy patients have unknown causes, there are factors in your lifestyle that can prevent the diagnosis of this condition and make sure your body stays healthy National Institute of Aging).
Conclusion

This is the reality for millions of epilepsy patients every day. Epilepsy isn’t just a seizure: the anxiety before, the isolation after, and the depression that follows all shape the quality of their lives. So if you or someone you love experience one or more symptoms of epilepsy, don’t hesitate to reach out to your doctor. This helps them diagnose the cause of the symptoms to prevent the worsening of this condition.

To learn more about epilepsy, reliable resources include NIH PubMed, National Institute for Health and Care Excellence NICE, and Epilepsy Canada. So as a team, let's work together to raise public awareness on this medical condition and the millions of epilepsy patients that face life-threatening challenges every day.

matthias-seuntjens.text: Abstract

Receiving an unexpected diagnosis involving defective blood cells infiltrating the bone marrow can feel intimidating. This summary describes multiple myeloma in clear, accessible terms. The text explains cellular mutation processes, standard diagnostic steps, key symptoms, and innovative immunotherapy methods. While many clinical articles bury vital information in complicated jargon, this text simplifies hematology concepts so families can better understand their treatment options and navigate care with confidence.
Introduction

Imagine visiting a doctor because your back hurts or, perhaps, because you have been feeling exhausted for a week or two. You are thinking that maybe you have injured a muscle or just need to rest. Suddenly, the routine blood tests that the doctor orders reveal that your white blood cells are attacking your own bone tissue: your healthcare journey is suddenly reshaped by a diagnosis of multiple myeloma.

Unfortunately, thousands of people receive such a diagnosis every year, and, for them, the disease comes as a terrible surprise. Let's talk about the basics of this condition and what a person should know about multiple myeloma to reduce the stress caused by the diagnosis.
Section 1: Causes and Risk Factors

First of all, to understand the disease, its origin needs to be studied. First, scientists note that the disease stems from acquired genetic changes within individual cells rather than an inherited trait. This blood cancer begins when a single plasma cell in the bone marrow undergoes genetic changes that cause it to proliferate uncontrollably Rajkumar, 2022. The altered cell produces abnormal antibodies and multiplies, replacing normal blood cells in the body with neoplastic tissue Cowan et al., 2022. As a result, the patient's body begins to produce huge amounts of monoclonal protein, M-protein, which circulates throughout the body and interferes with the function of healthy cells Cowan et al., 2022. At the same time, science has not yet discovered exactly which specific genetic triggers cause these cellular changes, so specific prevention strategies for multiple myeloma remain difficult to outline.

However, doctors have identified certain population groups that are more likely to develop multiple myeloma. This disease is most commonly diagnosed in older adults, with an average patient age of 65 or older Rajkumar, 2022. In addition, men are more likely to develop multiple myeloma than women.

Finally, scientists have found significant racial disparities in the prevalence of multiple myeloma: people of African descent are more likely to develop this disease, and on average, they are diagnosed at a younger age than white individuals Rajkumar, 2022. Because of this, researchers are focusing their efforts on reducing healthcare inequalities to ensure that all patients receive timely and appropriate care for multiple myeloma Rajkumar, 2022.
Section 2: Signs & Symptoms

Multiple myeloma is a systemic disease that affects the entire body, but since its neoplastic cells grow inside the bone marrow, the symptoms that a patient experiences can be somewhat confusing. A helpful tool in understanding multiple myeloma is the mnemonic CRAB, which stands for Calcium elevation, Renal failure, Anemia, and Bone pain Mohty et al., 2024. Using this diagnostic framework, one can better understand the bodily changes that occur as multiple myeloma develops.

First, damaged bones break down and release excess calcium into the bloodstream, causing hypercalcemia, which leads to severe thirst, vomiting, or mental confusion Mohty et al., 2024. Next, as abnormal plasma cells proliferate and M-proteins accumulate, they interfere with kidney function, causing roughly 42% of patients to suffer from renal failure or damage Mohty et al., 2024. Furthermore, neoplastic cells suppress bone marrow activity and disrupt red blood cell production, causing anemia that leaves approximately 73% of patients with severe fatigue and shortness of breath StatPearls, 2024. Finally, rogue cells directly weaken bone tissue, leading about 58% of patients to report intense back or chest pain as a primary symptom of the condition StatPearls, 2024.
Section 3: How Doctors Diagnose It

Unfortunately, multiple myeloma often remains asymptomatic until doctors suspect it based on routine blood tests. For example, patients may have a routine examination and tests when visiting a doctor, and abnormal results may indicate a suspicion of multiple myeloma Cowan et al., 2022.
Blood and urine tests are typically the first steps in diagnosing multiple myeloma. In particular, doctors search for abnormal light chains in the urine or M-protein in the blood Cowan et al., 2022.

However, to confirm a diagnosis of multiple myeloma, a bone marrow biopsy is required. During this procedure, a specialist takes a small sample of liquid bone marrow from the posterior iliac crest using a special needle Cowan et al., 2022. Patients are under local anesthesia during the procedure and do not feel pain. The cells that the doctor removes are studied under a microscope: if these abnormal plasma cells take up 10% or more of the marrow, it indicates multiple myeloma Cowan et al., 2022. In addition, imaging techniques such as X-ray, CT, or MRI scans are frequently used to determine the exact location and extent of bone damage.
Section 4: Treatment & Management

Anyone who has been studying multiple myeloma knows how scary the early 2000s were for patients with this diagnosis. Fortunately, modern medicine has developed a set of effective treatments that allow doctors to fight multiple myeloma for as long as possible after diagnosis.

Today, the treatment of multiple myeloma is largely based on a combination of methods, including targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and stem cell transplantation Moreau et al., 2023. Targeted therapies make it possible to block specific substances needed for the growth and proliferation of malignant cells Moreau et al., 2023. Meanwhile, immunotherapy drugs target tumor cells directly to allow their selective destruction by the body's immune system Moreau et al., 2023. In addition, stem cell transplantation allows doctors to collect healthy blood-forming cells from the patient, expose the body to therapy to destroy the malignant cells, and return the healthy cells to rebuild the marrow Moreau et al., 2023.

Beyond these traditional methods, doctors are testing new treatments such as CAR-T cell therapy, which involves modifying healthy T cells so that they can recognize and destroy tumor cells Moreau et al., 2023.
Section 5: Living With Multiple Myeloma

The most important aspect of managing multiple myeloma is treating it as a chronic disease. Doctors recommend that patients take individualized measures to maintain their quality of life and reduce physical burden.

Under medical guidance, many patients are advised to monitor and increase their fluid intake, as proper kidney function is critical to help flush out excess fluid containing M-protein and calcium. This is especially important if the patient has already experienced hypercalcemia or renal insufficiency.

A second crucial step in living with multiple myeloma is protecting the body from physical stressors. While strenuous sports and heavy weightlifting should generally be avoided due to bone fragility, staying moderately active helps stimulate blood circulation and maintain bone density. Supporting immune system health is equally critical, given the increased risk of infection for people with multiple myeloma: it is essential to take active measures to avoid viral infections.
Finally, it is important to remember that having multiple myeloma is not a reason to give up: patients are encouraged to maintain a positive outlook and enjoy fulfilling lives.
Conclusion

Facing a diagnosis of multiple myeloma brings understandable uncertainty for patients and their loved ones. However, one should not despair when faced with this diagnosis, as modern medicine has made significant strides in fighting this disease. In particular, researchers have developed powerful immunomodulatory drugs that have transformed treatment options. Therefore, as endorsed by Aware in Medicine, one should remember that the primary weapon in the fight against multiple myeloma is knowledge, the essential tool for patients to stay strong when facing this disease.

Acne vulgaris is a skin condition that affects 85% of adolescents aged between 12-24 years old. Acne is not only a physical skin condition, but it can also build into psychological distress. This overview dives deep into the root causes of common acne, from sebum production to lifestyle and habits, while also breaking down symptoms, severities, and different treatment pathways. This overview connects the biology of acne with the emotional health aspect to help readers seek early treatment and feel good in their skin again.
Introduction

Imagine standing in a classroom, a coffee shop with a friend, or even a meeting, trying to learn or laugh. Instead, you’re following people's eye contact and body language, trying to see if they notice your acne or scarring. If this situation seems familiar, you are not alone. Acne vulgaris affects around 9% of the world's population, 85% of which are between 12-24 years old, which means this is one of the most common skin conditions in the world Tan J.K.L., Bhate K 2015.

Acne vulgaris (also known as common acne) is a chronic inflammatory disease of the hair follicle-sebaceous gland (the skin's natural pairing of a hair follicle and its attached oil gland). This skin condition appears when the hair follicles are blocked with excess sebum (oil) and dead skin cells, creating inflammation and breakouts.

This skin disease affects people not only physically, but also carries an emotional weight. Since acne vulgaris is a visible skin disease, one’s self esteem and confidence can easily be lost. For most individuals who do not struggle with acne, actions like leaving the house seem simple, but for those who do struggle, leaving the house can seem overwhelming by thinking about who they're going to see or how much of their acne they will have to cover up.

The root causes of common acne that we will be discovering today are hormonal changes, excess sebum production (excess oil), inflammation, genetics and lifestyle and environmental triggers. All of these causes can induce or aggravate this skin condition. The development of acne involves:
Root causes

Hormonal triggers & Excess sebum production: When locally produced or circulating androgen hormones (ex: testosterone) attach to the androgen receptors in the sebaceous cell (oil gland cell), oil production is triggered. The excess oil gets trapped in the pores which causes inflammation. This process is especially active during hormone imbalance, pregnancy, fluctuates during the menstrual cycle and puberty Zoubilis C.C., Degitz K. 2004.

Genetics: Genetics contributes to approximately 81% of the risk towards progress in this skin disease Bataille V et al 2002. Although there is not a specific acne gene, it is considered a polygenic (disease that is influenced by multiple genes) condition that is inherited. The trait inherited dictates the oil production, skin cell shedding and inflammatory responses Zhang H, Zhang Z 2023.

Lifestyle & Environmental triggers: One's environment and daily activities heavily affect acne vulgaris. Lifestyle habits that can trigger acne vulgaris are high sugar foods such as sugars, processed carbohydrates, white bread, and dairy products that trigger your insulin levels to spike resulting in excess oil production and inflammation. Poor hygiene (ex: not washing off sweat and germs such as cutiebacterium acnes C. acnes)), allowing sweat, dirt, and oils to rest on your skin after a workout or high intensity activity will quickly result in clogged pores. Stress and lack of sleep, elevate your cortisol (stress hormone). Elevated cortisol causes excessive sebum production and aggravates acne. Environmental factors include humidity, overexposure to the sun and to pollution also plays a significant role in triggering breakouts Deng Y, Wang F, He L 2024.

Signs & Symptoms of Acne Vulgaris: The two main categories of acne are inflammatory and non-inflammatory. Inflamed acne presents itself with papules (small and solid raised bump), pustules (raised bump that contains visible pus), and cysts (sacs filled with fluid or semi solid substances)(Eichenfield D.Z., Sprague J, Eichenfield L.F. 2021 ; Fox L et al 2016. Inflammatory acne occurs when there is too much excess sebum in the blocked hair follicles causing inflammation. The symptoms of non-inflammatory acne are open comedones (blackheads) and closed comedones (whiteheads). These symptoms occur because the hair follicle is clogged with dead skin cells and excess oil.

Identifying the type of acne you might have is important to start the treatment pathway: Non-inflammatory: To identify non-inflammatory acne vulgaris symptoms we need to observe the open and closed comedones. An open comedone means that the pores are dilated (open) and are being exposed. Open comedones are more commonly referred to as “blackheads”. Blackheads are visibly black because there are trapped dead skin cells and oil in your pores. This trapped mixture then reacts to oxygen causing the mixture to “oxidize” causing the trapped material to change colors. This process is similar to when fruits like apples or bananas turn brown after sitting out in open air. “Whiteheads” can also be a symptom of non-inflammatory acne. Whiteheads are closed comedones meaning they stay under a thin layer of your skin. This allows the oil to be protected from open air, resulting in having a white appearance Wong C.M. et al 2024.

Inflamed acne: To identify inflammatory acne vulgaris symptoms we need to observe if papules, pustules, nodules and cysts are present Zaenglein A.L et al 2016. Papules are small, firm, bumps with a “red border”. Often, they are tender when touched.

Pustules are commonly known as pimples. They are developed directly on top of papules. They are fluid filled with a white or sometimes yellow hue pus. Nodules are large and painful lumps that go deep past the outer surface of the skin. Nodules do not have a “head” unlike pustules or whiteheads. They are rather firm and very inflamed. Cysts are deep fluid filled bumps that are very painful and are highly common to cause scarring.
Diagnosing Acne Vulgaris

Diagnosing acne vulgaris is commonly done by a clinical examination. The doctor will look for acne characteristics such as open comedones (blackheads), pustules, inflamed papules, closed comedones (whiteheads), and nodules and cysts. Depending on which of the acne vulgaris characteristics are present, acne is classified into three different severity categories: mild, moderate and severe. These classifications serve as a guide to decide which treatment pathways are the most appropriate Eichenfield L.F. et al 2013.
Note: Symptoms vary widely between individuals; readers should not self-diagnose based on this list. If someone suspects they have this condition, they should consult a healthcare provider.

Treating and Managing Acne Vulgaris: Depending on the severity of acne vulgaris there are many different treatment options such as topical therapies (tretinoin), benzoyl peroxide, azelaic acid (topical medication that reduces inflammation), or combinations of topical treatments. Mild acne can be managed using these fixed-dose topicals. These treatments help the clogged hair follicles and surface-level characteristics. According to the National Center for Biotechnology Information, mixing topical treatments like benzoyl peroxide with a retinoid such as tretinoin (a Vitamin A medication) can be more effective than either of the treatments alone. It is important to note that patients should always follow the doctor’s recommendation instead of trying treatments spontaneously.

When the severity of acne is between moderate and severe, treatment progresses from topical skincare to oral medications and treatments. These oral medications help to reduce inflammation that the topical skincare cannot treat alone. For women, sometimes hormonal medication is prescribed, such as contraceptive pills or spironolactone (medication that reduces the effects of androgens in some women)
which help regulate sebum production mediated by androgens Reynolds R.V. et al 2024.

When acne is severe and involves scarring, nodules & cysts, or treatment-resistant acne (acne that fails to clear up after standard treatments), then oral isotretinoin is the most effective treatment pathway. Since oral isotretinoin has a high success rate, the guidelines advise to start the medication as early as possible to minimize permanent scarring Keow S, Xiong G, Abu-Hilal M 2025.
Living with Acne Vulgaris

Severe acne vulgaris can often be painful due to the inflamed nodules and cysts Hazarika, N. & Archana M, 2016. Since nodules and cysts are deep in our skin layers, they create pressure and inflammation making it very uncomfortable for simple daily facial movements such as speaking, chewing or even smiling. In addition, nodules and cysts may lead to permanent scarring Zhou C et al 2023. Scarring can cause psychosocial morbidity such as depression and suicidality Xu S et al 2021.

Physical facial changes such as acne and scarring can trigger depression, social detachment and suicidality Gupta N et al 2023. Understanding that the struggles of acne are not only physical but also have a huge emotional toll is critical Hazarika, N. & Archana M, 2016. Early treatments will help prevent permanent scarring and the mental health impacts. Zhou C et al 2023.

Dealing with acne vulgaris goes far beyond the surface of the skin and deliberately impacts mental wellbeing. The continuous presence of breakouts can feed into personal insecurities and lead to social withdrawal. Recognizing the emotional toll acne vulgaris is vital for treatment approaches, as reducing these wellbeing burdens is just as important as clearing physical symptoms.
Emphasize: Treatment plans are highly individualized; readers should always consult their personal physician before starting or modifying treatment.
Conclusion

Acne vulgaris is one of the most common skin diseases, affecting 9% of the world's population in a physical and mental manner. Luckily, there now have been many studies and new treatments to make acne more manageable. Through ongoing clinical research, there is an advancement in treatments, holistic care and knowledge on acne vulgaris allowing us to have a bigger picture of what this disease is and also a wider range of treatment options. With the resources we have accessible today, early clinical treatments allow effective solutions, helping patients manage their acne, minimize scarring but also to feel more confident, empowered and able to take back control of their quality of life.
