olivia-wang.text: Abstract

Most people view diabetes as “eating too much sugar” or “always taking insulin injections,” but it is much more than that. The world doesn’t understand that more than 830 million people worldwide are affected by type 2 diabetes, yet more than 50% of them are still left undiagnosed. People should gain more knowledge about this condition to prevent and treat it. That is exactly what this article will give readers: a guide to understanding type 2 diabetes, its causes, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment and next steps. Stop wondering what to do about diabetes and start being the answer.
Introduction

Type 2 diabetes affects more than 830 million people worldwide and 50% of them remain still undiagnosed. According to the research Mayo Clinic, section 1 we can determine that type 2 diabetes is a chronic disease that alters the procedure of breaking down glucose, a type of sugar that gives energy to our cells. For people not affected by diabetes, the glucose is broken down and enters the bloodstream, increasing the sugar level in the blood. To compensate for the rise, insulin is added, an essential hormone produced by the pancreas that stimulates glucose to enter cells for storage and energy Cleveland Clinic, section 2.

For those with type 2 diabetes, this process of digesting glucose doesn’t function as well and requires external regulations. It is triggered by two main factors: the inability of the pancreas to produce enough insulin and the body’s weak response to it.
Becoming less sensitive to the insulin signal is known as becoming insulin resistant.

According to research Global Self Healthcare Education and Research, section 5, as a result of the weakened signal from the target tissues in the skeletal muscles, liver, and fats, the body tells the pancreas to produce excessive insulin, which builds up in the blood. The weakened signal and its receptor, a special protein on the cell surface unlocking specific structures, act as a key trying to open a coated lock. Since the pancreas wants the glucose to enter the coated cells anyways, it decides to force more insulin against the cells. Over time, the pancreas loses the ability to produce this hormone and requires insulin injections.

At first, there are minor symptoms that often go unnoticed: weight loss, blurred vision, frequent thirst, urination, hunger, and craving sugar. Your body is trying to tell you that there is a problem with your pancreas and that you should bring attention to it. If you ignore those symptoms, massive amounts of glucose may start to build up in the bloodstream, elevating the chance for future life-threatening disease, like cardiovascular and neurological complications. That’s why understanding this disease can help you control your blood sugar level and prevent fatal damage.
Causes

1 in 3 adults are most likely to have diabetes during their lifetime, according to UW Medicine, section 1. Although type 2 diabetes is partly genetic, it is more commonly caused by lifestyle factors and age. Genetics play a role in the family history of type 2 diabetes, obesity or the thousands of gene variants that affect the processing of glucose. However, this disease weighs more on age, gender and lifestyle, like diet, stress level and living environment. A 70 year old man who works in a factory and eats BeaverTails every night statistically has a higher risk of type 2 diabetes than a 20 year old female who works in a hospital and cooks home-made food.
Risk Factors
Other than age, gender and lifestyle, statistics show prominent risk factors for this disease.

- Being prediabetic - Having high cholesterol - Having a high blood pressure - Having a family history of diabetes - Being Indigenous, African, East Asian, South Asian - Living as a middle-income class 11% vs. a low-income class 7% What Brings You a Step Closer… According to a Harvard Health study, having fried foods every day increases the risk of type 2 diabetes by 50%, as it leads to the three main causes of diabetes: weight gain, high cholesterol and high blood pressure. Eating foods high in saturated fat, like milk or red meat also enhances the chance of type 2 diabetes, playing a part in insulin resistance. Worst of them all, sugary foods or drinks, causing glucose to rapidly spike and your pancreas to release big amounts of insulin. This will eventually lead to the loss of the ability for this organ to produce insulin.
Believe it or not, high levels of stress can also increase the risk of type 2 diabetes.
When a person is stressed, cortisol and adrenaline are released, which are the body’s primary stress hormones. Glucose is then dumped into the bloodstream, making you feel the burst of energy.

People who live in an atmosphere with little air pollution and a lot of green space will more likely walk and do physical activity. A person living close to a supermarket is also more probable to cook organic food at home.

Symptoms & Different Stages of Type 2 Diabetes Insulin resistance: Developing insulin resistance is the first stage of type 2 diabetes and will most likely not result in any change. As one of the main causes of type 2 diabetes, the pancreas doesn’t pick up a strong enough signal that directs it to produce a certain amount of insulin. At this stage, the pancreas is already starting to act on unusual activity and blood sugar levels are slowly going to rise.

Prediabetes: At this stage, people may notice mild symptoms, like blurred vision, weight loss, frequent thirst, hunger, urination and craving sugar, or none at all. This explains why 73% of patients are left undiagnosed and could have been living with this disease for many years already. If you feel any of these symptoms, it’s best to check in with a doctor to diagnose whether or not you are prediabetic to create a medical plan.
The only way to find out is by taking a blood test called the Hemoglobin A1C test.

According to research Gunther, section 2; UW Medicine), blood sugar levels residing between 100 milligrams/deciliter (mg/dL) and 125 mg/dL means that someone is prediabetic and may face future complications with type 2 diabetes.

Compared to the later stages, this condition is reversible and if people become more aware about their lifestyle, they can become non-prediabetic. However, once you no longer show a high blood sugar level, you should maintain that level, because if you were prediabetic, there is a higher chance that you can become one again.
Type 2 Diabetes: As a person enters the earlier stages of type 2 diabetes, these symptoms get more noticeable, as their blood sugar levels rise above 126 mg/dL.
Adding on to the symptoms listed in prediabetes, you may also start experiencing tingling or numbness in the feet or hands and wounds that take a long time to heal.
Now, the pancreas is exhausted due to insulin resistance and starts to produce less and less insulin.

Type 2 Diabetes with Complications: However, when this disease progresses to the later stages, it is too late. You have had type 2 diabetes for many years now and you still haven’t got it treated. Based on Govindarajan Venguidesvarane et al., section 1, this situation accounts for over 80% of the population in a Rural Health Center and most of them got diagnosed at this stage, This condition is responsible for many complications, like blindness, since the blood vessels in the eyes start to swell up due to the excess glucose. This damages the vessel walls and leaks fluid and blood into the eye.

The most common complications are heart attacks or strokes: when the excess glucose mixes with fat and cholesterol in the blood and forms plaques. This blocks the blood from flowing freely and eventually stops the circulation.

Nevertheless, the most rare but probable, is when the body is no longer able to fight infection due to the damage done to white blood cells. This causes people to have to amputate their wounds in order to prevent life-threatening infection from spreading.
Note: Symptoms vary widely between individuals; readers should not self-diagnose based on this list. If someone suspects they have this condition, they should consult a healthcare provider.
Diagnosis
Diagnosis is your lifesaver. Type 2 diabetes is known as a “silent killer,” which is why you have to get tested with a Hemoglobin A1C test every few months at the clinic.
Listed below are the ranges of normal, prediabetic and diabetic blood sugar concentration.

- Normal = less or equal to 100 mg/dL - Prediabetic = 100 mg/dL 125 mg/dL - Diabetic = more or equal to 126 mg/dL This could also be done daily using a glucometer at home, a portable medical device to measure blood sugar level. First, you would insert the test strip into the glucometer.

Next, use the lancet, or tiny blade, to prick the side of your finger and collect a droplet of blood onto the tip of the strip. Read the number on the glucometer and assess your blood sugar concentration.
Other tests also exist to identify type 2 diabetes, such as the diabetic foot examination.

When a person has type 2 diabetes, they often lose the ability to feel the endings of their nerves. An expert will first use a plastic thread and put pressure to different parts of your foot to make sure that the nerve endings are still functioning. Then, they will put a 128 Hertz Hz tuning fork, a medical tool, onto the corner of both feet to confirm that you can feel the vibration.

Before being diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, doctors might assess the patient’s medical history to bring out an accurate diagnosis and make sure that the context fits in. They also consider their family history, the symptoms being experienced and any physical abnormalities, like obesity, hypertension and eye hemorrages. Their immunization history might as well be taken into account to analyze the level of strength of the patient’s immune system, as diabetes highly compromizes it.
Treatment

If a person is diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, doctors might offer different treatment options to avoid future complications. Depending on certain stages, there will be specific procedures to take. However, regardless of the stage, a person should try to treat the following conditions if experienced: Hypertension: According to research Orrange, section 3, hypertension could be treated with a daily intake of prescription medications. One type of medication includes the angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor or ACE inhibitor. Its function is to prevent the formation of angiotensin II, a hormone that increases blood pressure.

Based on research NIH, section 2; Orrange), modifying your diet can also be very helpful, such as following the DASH diet, consisting of plenty of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, low-fat dairy, vegetable oils and lean meats. Limiting alcoholic beverages, sugary drinks and red meats is recommended.

Plaque Buildup: According to research Harvard Health Publishing, section 3, doctors often prescribe statins, medications that block the liver enzyme from producing cholesterol. Cholesterol is the one that if consumed excessively, builds up in the inner side of the arteries to create plaques. As a result, you may experience shortness of breath or chest pain.
In addition, there is a possibility that the plaque could rupture, causing a heart attack.

When a plaque ruptures, the substance filled with cholesterol, calcium and white blood cells seeps into the bloodstream and the body starts to create blood clots. This cuts off the circulation to vital organs, like the heart, brain and lungs.
Emphasize: Treatment plans are highly individualized; readers should always consult their personal physician before starting or modifying treatment.
Management
For individuals with insulin resistance or that are prediabetic, there are a few steps that can control their blood sugar level and prevent the occurrence of this condition.
As mentioned before, these include maintaining a healthy body weight, since it minimizes the blockage of the “lock” of the cell, allowing glucose to enter the cell for storage.

Maintaining a healthy diet was also very important. Minimizing foods high in sugar, cholesterol and saturated/trans fats as well as processed foods can lower the chance for cardiovascular and neurological conditions.

And most importantly, adapting lifestyle factors and increasing physical activity. This will lower blood sugar levels with the help of proper digestion of glucose and its efficient conversion to energy.
Richard’s Story
“I’m Richard King and I’ve lived comfortably with type 2 diabetes for over 20 years,”
King states, according to NKC Health).

When he was first diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, his mind immediately went through all the possible risks and dangers that he could encounter. The main dangers being heart attack or stroke, kidney failure and nerve damage. From then on, he decided that he wasn’t going to let diabetes determine his fate and went on to adapt his lifestyle and diet. After increasing physical activity and drastically changing eating habits nearly every day, he lost 30 pounds the next time he visited his physician, Dr. Dunbar.

King wanted to be a healthy individual, despite his condition of type 2 diabetes and he sends a message to inspire those experiencing any stage of diabetes: if you don’t feel well, don’t ignore these indications and go to the doctor. King consulting with Dr.

Dunbar as one of the best decisions that he has ever made during this journey. She stepped in King’s shoes and understood his health concerns and gave in her thoughts of how to manage his condition for the future.

One piece of advice that he gave to himself was to always have a clear ruler in his head telling you to constantly change your diet and lifestyle factors. No matter how strong the urge to experience what you had before is, the urge to become a healthier individual should be stronger.

This led him to his final message which was to maintain your blood sugar level on a regular basis by checking with a glucometer. This will allow you to understand your current stage and figure out your next steps onwards.
Now What?

In the current world, we are able to understand type 2 diabetes, diagnose this condition, as well as treat it, and maintain a healthy condition afterwards. According to research Shomali, section 1, in future years, scientists are looking at an increase of type 2 diabetes cases as people become more inactive through the convenience of technology. Even though physicians and experts continuously remind patients to maintain a healthy lifestyle, patients never seem to follow their instructions until they experience the consequences. This means that diabetes will slowly become part of our lives and the research that is being conducted is essential for the future.
“Having diabetes might not be your choice, but managing it is,” Advocators). Type 2 diabetes is a treatable and manageable disease that is empowered by your own hands.

This disease is one that you inevitably live with your entire life and it is totally up to you whether you want to change that. Becoming a healthier person and adapting your lifestyle is a hard decision, but it is one that your later self will thank your current self for. Be that person: see a doctor, diagnose your disease and get treatment. Remember, “diabetes may be tough, but you are tougher,” Advocators).

sophia-bhatti.text: Abstract

Endometriosis is a chronic inflammatory disorder affecting up to 10% of women worldwide, which is heavily under researched. This condition consists of tissue resembling the cells lining the uterus migrating to other parts of the body, forming lesions and scarring much like cancer. These lesions inflame, and can cause a myriad of symptoms, all depending on the patient. This condition can affect any area of life, from fertility to mental health, and hasn't received the attention it deserves despite its potentially detrimental impacts. For decades, the medical community has dismissed the disorder and overlooked women's health. In this article, not only are the physical symptoms discussed, but the barriers women with endometriosis face today, the mental toll it takes, and what exactly has stopped us from finding a cure.
Introduction

If you follow any biomedical engineers or healthcare professionals on social media, you have no doubt seen outrage expressed towards the lack of resources going towards women’s health and research, particularly chronic conditions. One of these conditions is endometriosis, a chronic inflammatory ailment, caused by the migration of cells resembling endometrial tissue outside of the uterus and leading to detrimental and multilateral side effects. From sexual function to mental health, endometriosis has a negative effect on many domains of life which leaves many feeling powerless and at the mercy of their disorder. This condition affects up to 10% of women worldwide, often going undiagnosed or mistreated due to systemic barriers and biases in healthcare Chauhan et al., 2022.

Endometriosis is not just a phenomenon seen in medical textbooks: it causes intense pain and suffering for many women worldwide. Nevertheless, this disorder has been consistently dismissed by medical researchers and denied grants. It eventually leads you to ask one question: ‘Why is this happening?’ The main explanation is that the medical system today still holds the ideals of yesterday, forcing marginalized groups to pay the price for medical negligence. The only way to combat the real-life barriers in healthcare we see today, is to take action. Whether it be raising awareness, or learning more about the condition to advocate for yourself, you can make a difference.
Signs and Symptoms

Endometriosis is unique in the symptoms it causes, both due to the disorder’s variability and of its unclear causes. A symptom that is common for many women living with endometriosis is dysmenorrhea, or painful periods Chauhan et al., 2022. When menstruation causes a high level of pain, it can usually be attributed to an overproduction of hormones, leading to lower back pain, heavy bleeding, longer menstrual phases and pelvic pain. Another key symptom is dyspareunia, which is pain during sex. There are two main types of dyspareunia, deep and superficial. Superficial dyspareunia is pain limited to the vaginal opening and the vulva. Deep dyspareunia, however, causes pain to radiate to the lower pelvis Chauhan et al., 2022. Other symptoms like infertility, chronic pain, impaired sexual function, internal bleeding and impaired function of certain systems (i.e. metabolic) are also integral parts of the disease.

This list of symptoms doesn’t apply to everyone, in fact, many women experience different symptoms based on the location of their endometrial lesions. For example, if a lesion is located in your digestive tract, you may have bloody stool during your menstrual cycle Yin et al., 2023. This is due to the endometrial cells in your gut shedding its lining, just like during your period. Nevertheless, patients may also be asymptomatic, or only display a limited amount of symptoms. Combined with the lack of knowledge concerning causes for symptoms, and the migration of tissue into many parts of the body, endometriosis is difficult for medical professionals to spot without imaging, analyzing saliva or invasive surgery with the training and technology at their disposal today.
Note: Symptoms vary widely between individuals; readers should not self-diagnose based on this list. If someone suspects they have this condition, they should consult a healthcare provider.
Causes and Risk Factors

Despite the overlooking of endometriosis in research, scientists have managed to narrow down causes and risk factors for the disorder in recent years. Many recent studies have successfully hypothesized some probable causes for endometriosis, with the main identified cause being something called retrograde menstruation Chauhan et al., 2022. Retrograde menstruation consists of cells from the uterine lining travelling up the fallopian tubes during the menstrual phase. Due to the fallopian tube not being physically attached to the ovaries, the tissue migrates to other parts of the abdominal cavity. This phenomenon also plays a role in ectopic pregnancies, meaning pregnancies where the fertilized egg migrates and grows in other parts of the abdominal cavity. Retrograde menstruation can happen to almost anyone with a cycle, and already happens to 76-90% of women with patent fallopian tubes, a term used to designate healthy tubes that allow ovum to travel through Chauhan et al., 2022. In recent years, researchers have succeeded in identifying risk factors with both loose and strong correlations. Firstly, there is an element of genetic predisposition. Recent research has shown that endometriosis tends to be observed in families, and therefore inherited Hansen & Eyster, 2010. Moreover, certain variables such as diet have been loosely correlated with endometriosis, demonstrating the potential link between trans fat and red meat consumption Arab et al., 2022.

Notwithstanding some research being done on this theorized link, it remains unproved as little research has been done. Furthermore, previous surgery in the lower abdominal area can increase the likelihood of endometrial cells spreading, causing something called ‘scar endometriosis’. For example, patients may be at risk after cesarean sections due to the possibility of tissue breaking away from the main incision and migrating to other parts of the body Chauhan et al., 2022. The large advancements in our knowledge about endometriosis is absolutely a cause for celebration. However, due to the newness of most recent research, certain domains have been underexplored and there is still much work to be done to fully understand this complex gynecological pathology.
Diagnosis

In the past, the only way women with endometriosis could obtain a diagnosis was through invasive procedures like exploratory surgery, or large surgeries where lesions were spontaneously discovered. Today, many advancements have been made in diagnosing patients with endometriosis that are more cost effective, less invasive and more efficient.

First and foremost, imaging is the most commonly used procedure to detect endometriosis. MRIs, ultrasounds, and other forms of medical imaging help greatly in identifying the locations and number of lesions, allowing for more targeted treatment and a personalized plan moving forward Mayo Clinic, 2024. Additionally, laparoscopy is another commonly used way to determine whether a patient has endometriosis. Through minimally invasive surgery assisted with a flexible camera, surgeons can perform operations in the abdominal and pelvic region with ease Mayo Clinic, 2024. This allows for lesions to be removed immediately, and is done after imaging has been performed to either eliminate the excess endometrial tissue or to further explore the cavity. Finally, new research has discovered that endometriosis can be detected through saliva analysis, looking for a microRNA (or miRNA marker that indicates the presence of endometrial lesions Nigdelis et al., 2024. Despite this treatment being revolutionary, it is still new and needs to be further explored before widespread implementation Nigdelis et al., 2024. This does not negate the huge importance of more minimally invasive avenues of diagnosis, particularly for adolescents or individuals who would be at risk or uncomfortable during invasive procedures.

Finding avenues of detecting endometriosis medically isn’t the greatest barrier for those possessing the disorder; it's the huge gap in time between experiencing symptoms and formal diagnosis. For many women, this means months of being referred between specialists just to be told the same thing from every one. Combined with the time it takes naturally for symptoms to be concerning, this wait time becomes painful and insufferable. Instead of walking into an appointment without knowing what you need to do to be screened, seek to learn more about what’s to come and what screenings you need to exhaust the possibility of endometriosis. There are many services which help clients to prepare questions for appointments, for example when a certain disease is to be the suspected cause of your symptoms. Advocating for yourself and your health is one of the most significant factors contributing to getting you the diagnosis to access the care you need, especially in a system where women’s reproductive health has only recently been made a priority.
Treatment

As of now, there has not been a discovered cure for endometriosis. But, the disorder is highly treatable through various methods such as surgery and hormonal treatments. These treatments often range depending on the stage of endometriosis, and where lesions are located. Like cancer, there are four stages of endometriosis, with Stage IV being considered the most severe Chauhan et al., 2022, depending on the amount of lesions and adhesions present. Stage I consists of small lesions (active tissue that is responsive to hormones) with no lesions (scar tissue that has become unresponsive to hormones). Stage II consists of lesions covering the surface of the ovaries, and some very mild adhesions, whilst Stage III entails the deepening of lesions on the ovaries and the potential spread of adhesions to the fallopian tubes and ovaries. Stage IV is the most severe stage, with dense adhesions and lesions all over the ovaries, fallopian tubes and endometriomas in the ovaries. Endometriomas are large ovarian cysts, filled with menstrual blood accumulated over time Chauhan et al., 2022. It is important to note that a specific stage doesn’t necessarily align with a set of symptoms, it only specifies the progression and appearance of the lesions, adhesions and endometrioma. These Stages are the basis for treatment, along with the patient’s goals pertaining to fertility.

For most cases of endometriosis, medical professionals opt for drug-based treatment plans before moving on to surgery if the case progresses Mayo Clinic, 2024. The main types of medicine administered to patients with endometriosis are painkillers, hormone-based treatments and fertility treatments. All of the following medications and treatments aim to balance or decrease the amount of hormones in your bloodstream, which tricks the lesions in the body into minimizing how much they inflame during flare-ups. Some aim to eliminate the menstrual cycle by simulating menopause, whereas others may also possess the ability to shrink endometrial lesions. Many treatments can also be administered at once, depending on dosage, the progression of the illness and what works best for each individual. If hormonal treatment fails, only then will your doctor suggest surgery to remove the lesions and/or endometrioma Chauhan et al., 2022.

The main options that a patient will be provided will most likely be laparoscopy or hysterectomy, depending on progression Stage I, II, III or IV and the fertility goals of the patient. Laproscopy, explained in a previous section, is a minimally invasive, camera assisted surgery where the abdominal cavity is lightly inflated and long tools are used to explore the site. This form of surgery aims to conserve the structures underneath it, and is usually offered to patients with mid stage endometriosis or patients who want children in the future. If removing the lesions and endometrioma laparoscopically is not possible, or the adhesions are too deep for a good turnout, the patient is usually offered the choice to attempt laparoscopic surgery or to undergo a hysterectomy. There are multiple types of hysterectomies depending on the size of the affected area, including an oophorectomy which is when the ovaries are completely removed Mayo Clinic, 2024. Depending on how the disorder has spread and your desired outcome, your medical professional will recommend the procedure that’s best for you. Remember that your needs come first, and that they should be reflected in the care that you are provided. If you are not given the care you request, do not be afraid to advocate for yourself. Whether it's bringing in someone else to your appointments to help push for opportunities you want to explore, or receiving a referral to another specialist, do what you must to receive the guidance, respect and care you deserve. Emphasize: Treatment plans are highly individualized; readers should always consult their personal physician before starting or modifying treatment.
Living with Endometriosis

Most of this text has discussed the overall symptoms, risk factors and physical tolls that endometriosis takes on those who have it, but living with this disorder is a different topic entirely. Symptoms have a much broader effect than just physical symptoms, they have a large impact on the daily life and the mental health of those who possess them. It deeply affects overall quality of life, social fulfillment and interactions with others. It may even negatively affect individuals financially, as endometriosis can make it difficult to even get out of bed. It can even complicate romantic relationships, due to impaired sexual function caused by the condition. In a study assessing the overall mental health of women with endometriosis before and after treatment, it was found that before treatment, “scores of patients with endometriosis were significantly diminished in comparison to controls, especially in general health, vitality, mental health, and emotional role functioning domains” Rempert et al., 2024. Moreover, 43.1% of women with endometriosis suffer from moderate to severe depression Rempert et al., 2024. This indicates an obvious disparity between those with and without endometriosis, and the profound effect chronic pain disorders can have on all areas of life. Luckily, after treatment, the same study saw that “surgical, pharmaceutical (estrogen-progestin), or combined intervention led to a significant increase in overall QoL scoring (p < 0.03, particularly in the domains of bodily pain, general health, and social functioning” Rempert et al., 2024.

You must be thinking that this is amazing, and that women only have to get treatment to see an improvement in mental health, especially after those promising results. However, the reality of this diagnosis isn’t as straightforward as you may think. Due to biases and limited research into the disorder, diagnoses are extremely difficult to receive, and requires extensive appointments with medical professionals. For many women, this is difficult to accomplish because of extensive referrals and long wait times in the public system. Combine this with infrastructure that has historically denied and dismissed the pain of women, and obtaining a diagnosis seems completely out of reach for most women. And for this reason, many women cannot access the care they need to help alleviate their debilitating symptoms.
Conclusion

After reading the bulk of this article, try imagining what life could be like for the 5-10% of women that have this disease. The chronic pain, the heavy periods, the crippling symptoms and the inaccessibility of a diagnosis. Working, eating and even sleeping are affected, with many endometriosis patients having negatively impacted sleep quality Rempert et al., 2024. Now, let’s come back to reality, where you’re back in your own body. Whether you’re part of that 5-10% or not, there is so much you can do to help those who are. You might not have endometriosis, but my hope is that you understand how it can take over the lives of millions without warning. Talking about it, supporting those who have it and advocating for better care can change their lives for the better. Advocacy is the catalyst for positive change, and that can only happen by joining and amplifying the discourse that exists today and one day, you might be part of the reason that something happens to help that 5-10% of women. Because in the end, endometriosis cannot simply be reduced to a pathology, because it has so much more gravity to those who live through it every day.

With more than 70% of high school students not getting the recommended 8-10 hours of sleep on school night, millions of teenagers are at risk for sleep deprivation (Uccella et al.). This article explores how daily habits, especially late night-screen use, can disrupt sleep and how insufficient sleep can affect concentration, emotional regulation and academic performance. By explaining how sleep deprivation is recognized and managed, this article gives teenagers practical knowledge to make informed choices about their sleep and protect their health and academic success.
Introduction

At 6-30 AM, the alarm clock blares, but the exhausted 16 year-old cannot move from their bed. After a night of scrolling and messaging, they managed to get only five hours of sleep. While this habit may seem harmless, this lack of sleep and screen use destroys adolescent health. Today, more than 70% of high school students do not get the recommended 8-10 hours of sleep on school nights, putting them at risk for sleep deprivation (Uccella et al.). But what exactly does this mean for their health?

Sleep deprivation occurs when you consistently fail to get the proper amount and quality of sleep needed for your body. Although common among teenagers, sleep deprivation can negatively affect not only energy levels, but also classroom concentration, academic learning, and school performance.
Why are Teens Losing Sleep?

Teenagers (individuals between the age of 13 and 19 are especially susceptible to sleep deprivation due to homework, extracurriculars, stress, part-time jobs, and early school start times. Since their daily schedules often clash with their need to sleep, many teens do not get their necessary 8-10 hours of sleep per night. At the same time, adolescence is a period when the body’s internal clock, also known as the circadian rhythm, naturally shifts later, which means that many teenagers feel tired later in the night, compared to younger children (Ja and Weiss). Together, this delayed “sleep drive” and their busy schedules can make it difficult for teens to get their proper rest on school nights.

One of the most prominent factors leading to sleep deprivation in teens is late-night screen use. Many students tend to use phones, tablets, or computers before bed to scroll through social media, message friends, play games, watch videos, or complete homework. In fact, roughly 60% of American children report regular use of devices during the hour before bedtime (Hale et al.). Although this habit may seem harmless or counterproductive, the blue light emitted by screens suppresses melatonin, the hormone responsible for the regulation of your circadian rhythm. When the production of melatonin is delayed, it is harder to fall asleep at a healthy time.

Furthermore, a recent literature review found that about 90% of included studies reported an association between screen use and delayed bedtime and/or decreased sleep time (Hale et al.). Screen use can significantly affect sleep by keeping the brain more stimulated when it should be winding down. Regularly receiving notifications or checking your phone in bed disrupts your body’s internal clock, making it much harder to fall asleep. As a result, late-night screen use often reduces both the duration and quality of sleep for teenagers (Hale et al.).

Although screen use is not the only cause of sleep deprivation, it is one of the most prevalent reasons for teenagers because it is built into daily life, often used when the mind should be shutting down. Understanding this connection is important because even small changes in your nighttime screen habits can improve sleep quality, helping teens concentrate better in class, strengthen their memory and support their overall academic performance.
What Happens When You Don’t Get Enough Sleep?

Sleep deprivation can affect much more than just a person’s energy levels. Although tiredness is the most obvious symptom, there are many more changes in teenagers’ daily performance, thinking, and emotions.

One of the most common signs of sleep deprivation is excessive daytime sleepiness: meaning that a person feels unusually tired during the day. This leads to a more difficult time concentrating during class, staying focused while studying, and participating in extracurricular activities. Research consistently shows that sleep loss causes the front part of the brain, the prefrontal cortex, to become sluggish and less active, severely reducing attention and hindering executive functioning, management skills handling memory, thinking, and impulse control (Killgore). During sleep, this area also actively replays the day’s events, strengthening important memories while removing unnecessary information in a process called memory consolidation (Seoane et al.). It allows students to retain what they learned during the day, but without enough quality sleep, the brain cannot effectively process or retain new information. Consequently, students may suffer from a slower reaction time, making more mistakes for tasks that require concentration and facing impaired decision-making. This combination of weak focus and poor memory consolidation ultimately forces students to spend more time studying while retaining less.

Sleep deprivation can also affect emotional well-being by reducing the brain’s ability to regulate emotions. This means that teenagers may experience heightened irritability, frustration, and a severely reduced tolerance to stress, causing them to overreact to everyday challenges. Research also shows that insufficient sleep may contribute to elevated anxiety levels and an increased vulnerability to stress and depressive symptoms (Shah et al.). Without 8-10 hours of sleep, students will react more strongly to negative events, making them more prone to anxiety or depression while also reducing motivation at school (McEwen and Karatsoreos). These emotional changes can affect relationships with family, friends, and teachers. Because several of these symptoms overlap with everyday stress, sleep deprivation can sometimes go unnoticed even when having a significant impact on life.

Although many of the effects of sleep deprivation, such as fatigue, difficulty concentrating, and bad moods, can appear after just a few nights of inadequate sleep, persistent sleep deprivation may also have long-lasting consequences on health.

Research has linked constant sleep deprivation to an increased risk of obesity, cardiovascular disease, cognitive decline, and poor mental health in life (Shah et al.). This suggests that sleep deprivation is more than just a short-term convenience; it has lasting effects on both physical and mental health.
Note: Symptoms vary widely between individuals; readers should not self-diagnose based on this list. If someone suspects they have this condition, they should consult a healthcare provider.
How is Sleep Deprivation Identified?

Although many medical conditions are diagnosed using a blood test or medical scan, there is no single test used to diagnose sleep deprivation. Instead, healthcare providers may use a combination of methods, including questions about a person’s sleep habits, symptoms, medical history, and daily routines. They may also use sleep diaries, questionnaires, or monitoring tools to assess sleep over time. If another sleep disorder or medical condition is suspected, additional testing, such as a sleep study, may be recommended.

The first steps in diagnosing sleep deprivation are discussing a person’s sleep schedule. Healthcare professionals begin by asking about a patient’s sleep schedule as everyday habits often reveal the underlying cause of sleep deprivation. Questions about bedtime, wake-up time, nighttime awakenings, and daytime fatigue help identify patterns that may not be obvious to the patients themselves. They may also recommend using a sleep diary, which is a daily record of sleep patterns, bedtime routines and daytime symptoms. By tracking sleep over several weeks instead of relying on memory, healthcare providers can identify recurring habits such as late night screen use or inconsistent bedtimes that contribute to poor sleep.

In certain cases, healthcare providers may recommend additional testing if they suspect another sleep disorder is the underlying cause. This may include one common test which is a polysomnography, also known as a sleep study, which monitors your brain waves, blood oxygen levels, breathing patterns, and eye movement while a person sleeps. Another tool is actigraphy, which involves wearing a small device similar to a wristwatch that tracks movement and sleep patterns over the course of several days or weeks. Unlike a single night in a sleep laboratory, actigraphy allows healthcare providers to accurately observe how a person’s sleep changes in their normal daily routine. Together, these tools give a precise diagnosis and help determine whether symptoms are caused by sleep deprivation or another underlying condition. Receiving a proper diagnosis is important because it gives healthcare providers the opportunity to provide the most appropriate treatments. Early diagnosis for sleep deprivation can also improve concentration, mood and daily functioning.
How Can You Get Your Sleep Back on Track?

Even if you are told by a doctor that you are not getting enough rest, the good news is that the condition can often be improved through healthy lifestyle changes. Because screen use is one of the most common contributors for teens, reducing screen use before bed is an effective first step since it allows melatonin levels to rise naturally and reduces the brain stimulation caused by social media. According to the American Academy of Pediatrics AAP, healthcare experts recommend that devices should not be allowed in children’s bedrooms and turned off 30 to 60 minutes before bedtime (Hale et al.). This gives a chance for the body to produce the sleep hormone, making it easier to fall asleep naturally.

Having a consistent nightly routine can also significantly improve both the quality and duration of sleep. Going to bed and waking up at the same time everyday, including weekends, trains your body’s circadian rhythm to expect sleep at consistent hours. As this routine becomes established, many teenagers experience a faster time falling asleep, deeper rest and better mood regulation. Other healthy habits include limiting caffeine later in the day, spending time outdoors, and keeping the bedroom cool 15-20°C ), comfortable, dark, and quiet (Hale et al.). Regular physical activity also supports better sleep by increasing the body’s natural drive to sleep after being awake throughout the day.

If sleep problems continue despite healthy habits, healthcare providers may prescribe medication such as sleeping pills. In some cases, persistent sleep deprivation may be a sign of an underlying sleep disorder such as insomnia or sleep apnea, which often require medical evaluation and treatment. Receiving appropriate care early can help prevent long-term effects on learning, mental health and physical well-being.
Emphasize: Treatment plans are highly individualized; readers should always consult their personal physician before starting or modifying treatment.

What It’s Like to Live on Too Little Sleep Living with persistent sleep deprivation can make everyday tasks more difficult than many teenagers realize. Tasks that once felt simple, such as paying attention in class, completing homework, and remembering information for a test, may require much more effort and energy to complete. Research has shown that academic performance correlated significantly to sleep quality (Seoane et al.). Constant fatigue can also make group projects, sport practices, music rehearsals, and afterschool jobs feel much more demanding. Even hobbies that teenagers normally enjoy may become exhausting, causing many students to lose motivation and confidence.

Sleep can also have important implications for long-term health. For example, findings suggest a 6 to 15% increased risk of death from any cause among individuals with insufficient sleep compared to those with adequate sleep (Shah et al.). Sleep deprivation causes severe physical consequences, including a weakened immune system, hormonal imbalance that trigger weight gain and increased inflammation. Over time, it significantly affects your cardiovascular system, drastically elevating risks for high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke and type 2 diabetes (Shah et al.).

Fortunately, sleep deprivation is often manageable once its causes are recognized. Small changes such as reducing nighttime screen use, following a regular sleep schedule, and creating healthier nightly habits, can improve sleep quality over time. For teenagers balancing school, activities, friendships, and responsibilities, prioritizing sleep is not a sign of laziness, but an investment in having the energy and focus to make the most of their day.
Sleep Isn’t Time Wasted

Sleep deprivation is more than simply feeling tired; it can affect a teenager’s ability to pick up new information, control your emotions and do well inside and outside the classroom. In other words, sleep is not just a time of rest, but it is essential to overall health. Fortunately, many of the most common causes of sleep deprivation, including late night screen use, are within a teenager’s control. By improving their sleep through small changes to bedtime habits, teenagers can protect their sleep. Getting enough sleep is not wasted time; it is one of the most important investments a teenager can make in their health, learning and future.
